rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all six peaks and identify the limiting separations while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Injection 1 already reached the maximum CRF, so test a shorter gradient while preserving its temperature and solvent window. The minimum resolution of 3.18 provides margin to shorten the separation without sacrificing full resolution.

Test the next shorter gradient to locate the full-resolution boundary. The closest pair is slope-sensitive, so this run will determine whether its current resolution of 2.03 survives another two-minute reduction.
Keep the six-minute gradient and increase temperature to test whether selectivity can rescue the limiting pair while shortening retention. The fully resolved eight-minute method remains the fallback.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness to lift the limiting resolution from 1.35 toward 1.5 while retaining a short separation. Keep temperature at 50 C because further heating may compromise the first pair, whose resolution has fallen to 2.17.

Raise the gradient window while preserving its slope to remove time spent at weak solvent and test starting-composition selectivity. Injection 5 already achieves maximum CRF; this tests whether full resolution can be retained with earlier elution.

Reduce the slope one grid step from injection 6 to recover the limiting pair's resolution while retaining the faster, higher starting composition. This should provide a shorter fully resolved separation than injection 5.

Trim the gradient to the observed elution window and raise the starting fraction, keeping the slope slightly shallower than injection 7. This tests a shorter separation while leaving the final organic fraction above the last peak's estimated elution composition.

Make the four-minute gradient slightly shallower to recover full resolution of the limiting pair, currently at 1.46. The endpoint remains comfortably above the last peak's estimated elution fraction of 0.51.

Shift the successful gradient window upward at constant slope to shorten retention further. This tests whether the first and central pairs retain full resolution as the first peak approaches the weakly retained region.

Reduce the slope from injection 10 to restore the central pair's resolution while retaining the faster starting composition. The first pair remains above 1.5, and the shallower gradient should also modestly improve its separation.

Test a steep gradient at lower temperature as an alternative selectivity regime that may separate the central pair after an elution-order reversal. The low starting fraction protects early retention, and injection 11 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Explore a shifted, steep gradient to change central-pair selectivity while keeping elution rapid. Raising temperature from the previous run should help separate the late pair, while the higher starting fraction tests a different central-pair separation regime.

Test a higher starting fraction with a shallower gradient to recover central-pair separation without spending time at weak solvent. Lowering temperature relative to injection 11 should help protect the early pair from excessive compression.

Test one temperature step above the fastest fully resolved method to see whether retention can be shortened while preserving maximum CRF. The early pair is the main risk, with resolution only 1.79 at 50 C.

Use the six-minute programming grid to obtain a slope between injections 8 and 9, targeting full resolution with less retention than injection 9. Return to 50 C because heating to 55 C compromised the early pair.

Test a small slope increase from injection 11, using the six-minute grid for finer adjustment than a four-minute gradient allows. This targets slightly earlier final elution while checking whether the central pair retains its narrow resolution margin.

Test whether a five-degree increase rescues injection 8's central pair and produces a faster fully resolved separation. The lower starting fraction than injection 15 should improve early-pair retention, although that pair remains the main risk.

Test a two-minute shallow gradient followed by a hold, aiming to preserve central-pair resolution with a shorter programmed ramp. The last peak will likely elute during the hold, so this run measures whether the lower endpoint introduces an unacceptable retention penalty.

Test the intermediate temperature at the higher starting fraction to measure whether central-pair selectivity improves while the early pair remains resolved. This isolates temperature relative to injection 14 and avoids the long final hold seen in injection 19.

With maximum CRF already secured, test a trimmed window that should give both critical pairs more resolution margin than the fastest method. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition, avoiding the prolonged hold seen in injection 19.

Raise the starting fraction from injection 21 while retaining its trimmed endpoint to shorten elution. This should provide more central-pair resolution margin than injection 11 while remaining faster than injection 21.

Test a cooler variant of injection 22 to increase early-pair separation while checking that the central pair retains full resolution. Injection 11 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method; this run evaluates a potentially more robust alternative.

Increase the endpoint one step from injection 23 to shorten retention while using its central-pair resolution margin of 1.95. This also tests whether the fastest fully resolved method from injection 11 remains fully resolved at a five-degree lower temperature.

Use a slope between injections 11 and 22 to target maximum CRF with more resolution margin than the fastest fully resolved method and less retention than injection 22. Keep 50 C, since cooler conditions weakened the central pair and hotter conditions compromised the early pair.
